messages.subject_clean: New CRAN release of mrds and Distance R packages
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance list,

We are pleased to announce the release of mrds version 3.0.0 and
Distance version 2.0.0 on CRAN.

Over the past months we have been working on improving performance when
fitting conventional distance sampling (CDS) detection functions - i.e.,
detection functions with distance as the only covariate.  The results of
this work is implemented in the new mrds version.  Most users will see
no change except perhaps for a speed-up in model fitting.  However,
users fitting functions with multiple adjustment terms or with
challenging data (such as overdispersed data that tends to come from
camera trap distance sampling data) may find improvements in model fit.
For such data we had previously recommended downloading the MCDS.exe
binary file, but this is no longer needed (although the option remains
available). Our thanks to Felix Petersma for leading this work on CDS
performance improvement.

Changing the optimization methods is judged enough of a change that we
have updated the major version number of the mrds package to 3.0.0.
Because the Distance package uses mrds for detection function fitting,
we have also updated this package's version number to 2.0.0.

For more details on the optimizer changes, see the package NEWS files:
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mrds/NEWS
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Distance/NEWS

As always, thank-you to those who have made feature requests or reported
issues. If you do find any problems, or want to suggest a new feature,
please feel free to raise an issue at either
https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/Distance/issues or
https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/mrds/issues

Lastly, advance notice that we have been working on a number of other
improvements to our distance sampling software and training: a new
version of Distance for Windows, an updated free online introductory
workshop and refreshed web pages including software examples.  We
anticipate making an announcement about all this in the next few weeks.

With best wishes,

Len Thomas
Distance development team

P.S. If you find you need to use the previous fitting algorithm, this is
possible with the ds() function in Distance using the argument
mono_method = "solnp" or with the ddf() function in mrds using the
argument control(mono.method = "solnp").

--

Hi,

I am just looking a the tee dataset and mrds model building. I was wondering why "distance" is taken into consideration in the mrmodel? In MRDS analyses we use the MR model to model sightability at the line and the DS model to model decay in detection at further distances from the plane.  So why use distances as a covariate for the MR model?

For example (page 45 of the document title "Package mrds"):
   xx <- ddf(mrmodel=~glm(formula=~distance*observer), dsmodel=~mcds(key="hn", formula=~sex), data=egdata, method="io", meta.data=list(width=4))

Thanks,

Lisa

messages.body_plain:
Lisa

The mark-recapture component of the MRDS modelling is a logistic regression fitted to the duplicate detections from independent observers. Because it is a generalisation of a Lincoln-Petersen mark-recapture estimator, it is sensitive to unmodelled heterogeneity; hence all possible sources of variation influencing the probability of duplicate detections need to be included in the models. One of those sources of variation could be distance from the transect--probability of duplicate detection could be influenced by distance from the transect.

Most published MRDS analyses include distance in the MR component in the candidate set.  For example, see the Buckland et al. (2015) book which includes analyses of Antarctic crabeater seals (Sect 5.4.2.1), North Sea minke whales (Sect 5.4.2.2) and Texas songbirds (Sect 5.4.2.3).

messages.body_plain:
Carlos

Multiple questions packed in this email.

DistWin offers several choices when dealing with animals in groups. The sample project "Stratify example"  contains survey data from animals in groups. In the window below, you can produce density estimates of individuals by multiplying group density by mean of observed groups or use the size-bias regression to adjust the group size estimate to account for size bias.

Yet another method is to use group size as a covariate in the detection function. This can be done in DistWin by choosing the MCDS engine and making the appropriate selections in this window below:

You can get the "Distance" R package to use either average observed group size (as you indicate) or include group size as a covariate in the detection function. The "Distance" R package does not offer the size-bias regression option as the current suggested approach for handling size bias is to include group size as a covariate in the detection function, thus

clever.hn <http://clever.hn> <- ds(data=risso, key="hn", formula = ~size)
I hope that answers your questions.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Density estimates of every species
messages.body_plain:
Sarah

The short answer to the apparent lack of density estimates in your output is simple. You have specified an Area in your data frame of 1. Remember the formula:

N = D*A

where N is abundance, D is density and A is area. When A=1, the D=N; so the reported abundance estimates are identical to the density estimates.

At a deeper level, note that you only have two replicate transects (implying your spatial inference is not very good) and your estimates of encounter rate variance is also not very good. Finally, your detection function model (with a parameter for each of your 56(?) species, cannot estimate those parameters well from a total of 157 detections across all species.

Look at the standard errors (and consequently the confidence interval widths) of your abundance estimates. Those measures of precision are telling you that you have so little information (few detections) that you have no confidence in the density of most of those species.

Just because it is possible to employ the "species as covariate" analysis, does not mean it is appropriate in all circumstances. The data you provide is too sparse (and the study design insufficiently intense) to produce species-specific estimates of density.

In some bird point counts that I did near a river some erosion took place and land disappeared into swift moving water. I think in a similar example with transect counts where part of the transects was to foggy to count a solution of reducing the transect length was suggested so I was wondering if there was an equivalent for point counts.

It might not matter to much but I was just trying to be through as this is a for my dissertation and it wasn't something we anticipated to happen but events like this aren't predictable.

Stephanie

Michael

Welcome to the list. Before we can deduce whether the software is doing the "right thing", we need to understand the design of your study. There is not enough information in your screen shots to  make your design obvious. In one screenshot you have an Area associated with your Regions, in other shots you do not.

Simply describe your study area, I believe you are calling it Peafowl District 13; what is its size? Include its area as a field in the Study Area layer.

How many transects did you walk when sampling your study area; your Word document output states there were 35 transects; is that accurate? One of your screenshots suggests each of the 35 transects are 896.6m in length. That sends up a flag for me; I would be surprised if spatially replicated transects are all the same length.

It seems more likely to me that you have a small number of transects (perhaps only a single transect) that you visited many times (28Jun2020, 12Jul2020, ...).

The effort of 88803.4 (Word document) doesn't seem to correspond to one of your screen shots (35 transects each of length 896.6, which would lead to effort of 31381m.

Once we get these details sorted, then we can ensure the data are correctly entered and the analysis can begin.

Meanwhile, have a look at some of the sample projects that come with the Distance for Windows software for ideas about data organisation. Have a read through the Users Guide, specifically Chapter 5 on data structures.

Dear distance-sampling list,

I am very pleased to announce new software, training and web site releases from CREEM:

Distance for Windows 8.0
This new version of our Windows-based software is distributed with a new msi installer, which removes difficulties associated with installing the software under the latest versions of Microsoft Windows. We have also included the latest versions of the distance sampling R packages for those using the R-based analysis engines.  We recommend users of Distance for Windows download the new version, available at  https://distancesampling.org

Free online training
We have created a completely new version of our free online course “Introduction to Distance Sampling”.  Content has been refreshed, lectures re-recorded and exercises updated.  We have added a new chapter on mark-recapture distance sampling.  The new course is available at https://distancesampling.org/online-course. This easy-to-navigate course website is structured to explore distance sampling concepts from fundamental through double observer methods for estimating detectability on the transect. It is searchable so concepts can be accessed easily to serve as a refresher.

messages.subject_clean: Help need for simulated extrapolation approach
messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance sampling community,

I am seeking assistance with simulating an extrapolation approach to estimate abundance within a management unit. Some parts of the area are inaccessible to our preferred survey platform, so I'm exploring extrapolation techniques. Before field testing, I would like to simulate this approach. Currently, the plan is to sample randomly placed subplots using line transects and extrapolate to the whole area based on environmental covariates.

Firstly, I'd appreciate feedback on the general approach, as I've found limited information on this topic and am still unsure if it's feasible. What are the key considerations when it comes to extrapolation?

Secondly, I've struggled to find code examples for extrapolation. A paper described the `dsmextra` package, but I couldn't locate the actual code. Are there any code examples available for extrapolation?

Lastly, I attempted to run simulations with multiple strata study areas, as outlined in the appendix A here: [https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html](https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html) <https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html%5D(https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html)>. I managed to create transects within these strata, but my simulations always fail.
This is an reproducible code example where `run.survey()` fails when the simulation uses multi strata.

```
# Load the required library

library(dsims)

# Create a detectability function

detect_uf <- make.detectability(

  key.function = "uf",

  scale.param = 0.8,

  truncation = 2

)

# Define the outer boundary and holes for the polygons

outer <- matrix(c(0,0,15,0,15,10,0,10,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

hole1 <- matrix(c(2,2,2,3,3,3,3,2,2,2), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

hole2 <- matrix(c(5,5,5,6,7,6,8,5.5,7,5,5,5), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

# Create polygons with holes

pol1 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer, hole1*1.5, hole2))

pol2 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 15, hole2*1.5 + 12))

pol3 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 30, hole2*2.5 + 20))

# Combine polygons into a simple feature collection

sfc <- sf::st_sfc(pol1, pol2, pol3)

strata.names <- c("SW", "central", "NE")

mp1 <- sf::st_sf(strata = strata.names, geom = sfc)

# Print the simple feature collection

print(mp1)

# Define the study area

area_m <- matrix(c(0,0,45,0,45,40,0,40,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

area <- sf::st_polygon(list(area_m))

# Plot the study area and the polygons

plot(area)

plot(mp1, add = TRUE)

# Create regions for the study area and subplots

study_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "study area", shape = area)

poly_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "sub plots", strata.name <http://strata.name> = strata.names, shape = mp1)

# Plot the regions

plot(study_region)

plot(poly_region)

# Create a flat density grid

density <- make.density(region = study_region, x.space <http://x.space> = 1, constant = 1)

# Add hotspots to the density grid for spatial variability

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(5, 5), sigma = 10, amplitude = 2)

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(15, 25), sigma = 5, amplitude = 3)

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(40, 15), sigma = 15, amplitude = -0.5)

# Plot the density grid

plot(density, study_region)

# Create a covariate list describing the distribution of cluster sizes

covariates <- list(cover = list(distribution = "ztruncpois", mean = 3))

# Create population descriptions for the study area and subplots

study_area_pop_desc_co <- make.population.description(region = study_region, density = density, covariates = covariates)

sub_plots_pop_desc_co <- make.population.description(region = poly_region, density = density, covariates = covariates)

# Create a systematic subplot design

subplots_design <- make.design(

  region = poly_region,

  transect.type = "line",

  design = "systematic",

  samplers = numeric(0), # OR

  line.length = numeric(0), # OR

  spacing = 3,

  design.angle = 0,

  edge.protocol = "minus",

  truncation = 2

)

# Generate transects for the subplot design

subplots_transects <- generate.transects(subplots_design)

# Plot the transects on the subplot region

plot(poly_region, subplots_transects, lwd = 0.5, col = 4)

# Create detection function analyses

ddf_analyses <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = c("hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2)

ddf_analyses_sub <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = c("hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2, group.strata = data.frame(design.id <http://design.id> = poly_...@strata.name, analysis.id <http://analysis.id> = rep("A", length(poly_...@strata.name))))

ddf_analyses_co <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~1, ~cover, ~cover), key = c("hn", "hr", "hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2)

ddf_analyses_sub_co <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~1, ~cover, ~cover), key = c("hn", "hr", "hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2, group.strata = data.frame(design.id <http://design.id> = poly_...@strata.name, analysis.id <http://analysis.id> = rep("A", length(poly_...@strata.name))))

# Create a simulation for the subplots

sim_sub <- make.simulation(

  reps = 99,

  design = subplots_design,

  population.description = sub_plots_pop_desc_co, # study_area_pop_desc_co, sub_plots_pop_desc_co

  detectability = detect_uf,

  ds.analysis = ddf_analyses_sub_co # ddf_analyses, ddf_analyses_sub, ddf_analyses_co, ddf_analyses_sub_co

)

# Run the survey and summarize the results

summary(sim_sub, use.max.reps = TRUE, description.summary = FALSE) # here were no successful repetitions.

# Failing

sub_survey <- run.survey(sim_sub) # Error in sample.int <http://sample.int>(length(x), size, replace, prob) : incorrect number of probabilities

# Print the survey results

print(sub_survey)

# Plot the survey results

plot(sub_survey, subplots)
```

BONUS questions: I'd like to assign a covariate to the individuals in the population based on their XY coordinates, to perform a sensitivity analysis of the effects of different levels of vegetation cover in the landscape.

Thank you very much for your time. Please let me know if you can provide guidance or share your experiences with these topics.

Best regards,

messages.body_plain:
Leonard

Welcome to the list. Quite a set of questions you have.

For model-based inference to be sound, the relationships found in modeling the data from the surveyed area is assumed to hold in the non-surveyed area. It is difficult to image how to assess that, given the non-surveyed area is inaccessible. Furthermore the distribution (in a statistical sense) of predictor covariates is assumed to be similar for the surveyed and non-surveyed areas. An example of a situation in which this would not hold: imagine the non-surveyed areas are inaccessible because they are extreme in altitude or terrain roughness. If those environmental covariates are used as predictors, it is unlikely the distributions will be similar in surveyed and non-surveyed areas.

Access to the code for the "dsmextra" package is described here

https://densitymodelling.github.io/dsmextra/

but I believe the package is no longer maintained. It depends on the deprecated "rgdal" package, which you might be able to install this way:

install.packages("rgdal", repos="http://R-Forge.R-project.org <http://r-forge.r-project.org/>")

Next, for you "dsims" simulation code. I haven't parsed all of your code. I think I might start with something slightly simpler, to make debugging easier. I see you are trying to use group size as a covariate. However a glance at this help page:

?dsims::make.population.description

flags up this

covariates
Named list with one named entry per individual-level covariate. Cluster sizes can be defined here, it must be named 'size'.
whereas you have the line:

# Create a covariate list describing the distribution of cluster sizes
covariates <- list(cover = list(distribution = "ztruncpois", mean = 3))

The error message states some problem with "probabilities", which is a bit vague, but might point to problems with the population.description.

I also don't know how you want your detectability function to behave, you specify that it should be a uniform key function, but you provide a scale.param, which the uniform key does not possess.

Finally, regarding your bonus question (to demonstrate I read your email through to the end), I do not believe "dsims" has the ability to assign covariates based upon coordinates of the simulated objects. At least I've not seen a demonstration of such abilities.
From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Leonard Hambrecht <leo...@hambrecht.phd>

Subject: [distance-sampling] Help need for simulated extrapolation approach

Hello Distance sampling community,

I am seeking assistance with simulating an extrapolation approach to estimate abundance within a management unit. Some parts of the area are inaccessible to our preferred survey platform, so I'm exploring extrapolation techniques. Before field testing, I would like to simulate this approach. Currently, the plan is to sample randomly placed subplots using line transects and extrapolate to the whole area based on environmental covariates.

Firstly, I'd appreciate feedback on the general approach, as I've found limited information on this topic and am still unsure if it's feasible. What are the key considerations when it comes to extrapolation?

Secondly, I've struggled to find code examples for extrapolation. A paper described the `dsmextra` package, but I couldn't locate the actual code. Are there any code examples available for extrapolation?

Lastly, I attempted to run simulations with multiple strata study areas, as outlined in the appendix A here: [https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html](https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html) <https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html%5D(https://distancesampling.org/dssd/articles/MultiStrataVignette.html)>. I managed to create transects within these strata, but my simulations always fail.
This is an reproducible code example where `run.survey()` fails when the simulation uses multi strata.

```
# Load the required library

library(dsims)

# Create a detectability function

detect_uf <- make.detectability(

  key.function = "uf",

  scale.param = 0.8,

  truncation = 2

)

# Define the outer boundary and holes for the polygons

outer <- matrix(c(0,0,15,0,15,10,0,10,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

hole1 <- matrix(c(2,2,2,3,3,3,3,2,2,2), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

hole2 <- matrix(c(5,5,5,6,7,6,8,5.5,7,5,5,5), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

# Create polygons with holes

pol1 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer, hole1*1.5, hole2))

pol2 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 15, hole2*1.5 + 12))

pol3 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 30, hole2*2.5 + 20))

# Combine polygons into a simple feature collection

sfc <- sf::st_sfc(pol1, pol2, pol3)

strata.names <- c("SW", "central", "NE")

mp1 <- sf::st_sf(strata = strata.names, geom = sfc)

# Print the simple feature collection

print(mp1)

# Define the study area

area_m <- matrix(c(0,0,45,0,45,40,0,40,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

area <- sf::st_polygon(list(area_m))

# Plot the study area and the polygons

plot(area)

plot(mp1, add = TRUE)

# Create regions for the study area and subplots

study_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "study area", shape = area)

poly_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "sub plots", strata.name <http://strata.name> = strata.names, shape = mp1)

# Plot the regions

plot(study_region)

plot(poly_region)

# Create a flat density grid

density <- make.density(region = study_region, x.space <http://x.space> = 1, constant = 1)

# Add hotspots to the density grid for spatial variability

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(5, 5), sigma = 10, amplitude = 2)

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(15, 25), sigma = 5, amplitude = 3)

density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(40, 15), sigma = 15, amplitude = -0.5)

# Plot the density grid

plot(density, study_region)

# Create a covariate list describing the distribution of cluster sizes

covariates <- list(cover = list(distribution = "ztruncpois", mean = 3))

# Create population descriptions for the study area and subplots

study_area_pop_desc_co <- make.population.description(region = study_region, density = density, covariates = covariates)

sub_plots_pop_desc_co <- make.population.description(region = poly_region, density = density, covariates = covariates)

# Create a systematic subplot design

subplots_design <- make.design(

  region = poly_region,

  transect.type = "line",

  design = "systematic",

  samplers = numeric(0), # OR

  line.length = numeric(0), # OR

  spacing = 3,

  design.angle = 0,

  edge.protocol = "minus",

  truncation = 2

)

# Generate transects for the subplot design

subplots_transects <- generate.transects(subplots_design)

# Plot the transects on the subplot region

plot(poly_region, subplots_transects, lwd = 0.5, col = 4)

# Create detection function analyses

ddf_analyses <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = c("hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2)

ddf_analyses_sub <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = c("hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2, group.strata = data.frame(design.id <http://design.id> = poly_...@strata.name, analysis.id <http://analysis.id> = rep("A", length(poly_...@strata.name))))

ddf_analyses_co <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~1, ~cover, ~cover), key = c("hn", "hr", "hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2)

ddf_analyses_sub_co <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = list(~1, ~1, ~cover, ~cover), key = c("hn", "hr", "hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2, group.strata = data.frame(design.id <http://design.id> = poly_...@strata.name, analysis.id <http://analysis.id> = rep("A", length(poly_...@strata.name))))

# Create a simulation for the subplots

sim_sub <- make.simulation(

  reps = 99,

  design = subplots_design,

  population.description = sub_plots_pop_desc_co, # study_area_pop_desc_co, sub_plots_pop_desc_co

  detectability = detect_uf,

  ds.analysis = ddf_analyses_sub_co # ddf_analyses, ddf_analyses_sub, ddf_analyses_co, ddf_analyses_sub_co

)

# Run the survey and summarize the results

summary(sim_sub, use.max.reps = TRUE, description.summary = FALSE) # here were no successful repetitions.

# Failing

sub_survey <- run.survey(sim_sub) # Error in sample.int <http://sample.int>(length(x), size, replace, prob) : incorrect number of probabilities

# Print the survey results

print(sub_survey)

# Plot the survey results

plot(sub_survey, subplots)
```

BONUS questions: I'd like to assign a covariate to the individuals in the population based on their XY coordinates, to perform a sensitivity analysis of the effects of different levels of vegetation cover in the landscape.

Thank you very much for your time. Please let me know if you can provide guidance or share your experiences with these topics.

Best regards,
Leonard

Just to augment what Eric said:  Distance for Windows can also deal with
data in latitude and longitude, but it's easier for most people to do
the projections outside of Distance.

Here is some information about it, in case anyone wants to go this route:

If you want to import the data in latitude and longitude, it has to be
in decimal degrees, not degrees-minutes-seconds format.  It's easy to
convert from one to another:

decimal degrees = degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3600

Once this is done, you can readily import the data into Distance using
the copy/paste method.  However, you then need to set a geographic
coordinate system for the layer (in Data layer properties, under the
Geographic data tab, click on Change coordinate system and then choose a
Geographic coordinate system from the drop-down), or (probably easier)
choose a default geographic coordinate system for the project before you
create any layers (File | Project Properties under the Geographic tab).
Also note that if you're doing survey design, you then need to define a
projection so that the design calculations can convert latitude and
longitude into x and y in meters for the purposes of creating designs.
(This is under design Properties, General Properties, Design Coordinate
System.)

More information about this is in the Users Guide, in Chapter 5 (Data in
Distance) under "Geographic (GIS) Data".

Hopefully this is useful.  Cheers, Len

Thank you for clarifying the model-based interference. We are planning to derive covariates from satellite produces, therefore we would know the statistical distribution of the covariates. The question that arises for me, should one prioritize randomly placing subplots within the accessible area, or priorities placing the subplots to cover as much of the statics distribution of the covariates?

Thanks for pointing me to the dsmextra vignette. It is unfortunate that dsmextra is no longer maintained.

Regarding my `dsims` code, I tried to simply it and removed the inclusion of covariates. Furthermore, I split the code into two clear examples. One creating a population and density for a larger area, but the transects are only being placed in the sample areas. And the second created a population and density for each sample area. However, both fail when trying to run the simulation. If the issue lies with the population.description, then I do not know what to change. I tried different things with the same result.
The scale.param in the uniform key function adjust the detection rate. A scale.param of 0.8 assumes an 80% detection rate, due to account for that not all animals are available for detection all the time. The only reason I chose a uniform function in this example is to keep it simple. You can try other function, but in my testing, this did not make a difference.

Please use this simplified code for your testing. There is some repetition in the code to ensure that both example can be run independently of each other.

```
### Example 1: Creating density and population for study_region and run simulation

# Load the required library
library(dsims)

# Create Multi Strata Region

# Define the outer boundary and holes for the polygons
outer <- matrix(c(0,0,15,0,15,10,0,10,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
hole1 <- matrix(c(2,2,2,3,3,3,3,2,2,2), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
hole2 <- matrix(c(5,5,5,6,7,6,8,5.5,7,5,5,5), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

# Create polygons with holes
pol1 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer, hole1*1.5, hole2))
pol2 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 15, hole2*1.5 + 12))
pol3 <- sf::st_polygon(list(outer + 30, hole2*2.5 + 20))

# Combine polygons into a simple feature collection
sfc <- sf::st_sfc(pol1, pol2, pol3)
strata.names <- c("SW", "central", "NE")
mp1 <- sf::st_sf(strata = strata.names, geom = sfc)

# Print the simple feature collection
print(mp1)

# Define the study area
area_m <- matrix(c(0,0,45,0,45,40,0,40,0,0), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
area <- sf::st_polygon(list(area_m))

# Plot the study area and the polygons
plot(area)
plot(mp1, add = TRUE)

# Create regions for the study area and subplots
study_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "study area", shape = area)
poly_region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "sub plots", strata.name <http://strata.name> = strata.names, shape = mp1)

# Plot the regions
plot(study_region)
plot(poly_region)

# Create a systematic subplot design
poly_design <- make.design(

  region = poly_region,
  transect.type = "line",
  design = "systematic",
  samplers = numeric(0), # OR
  line.length = numeric(0), # OR
  spacing = 3,
  design.angle = 0,
  edge.protocol = "minus",
  truncation = 2
)
# Generate transects for the subplot design

poly_transects <- generate.transects(poly_design)

# Plot the transects on the subplot region

plot(poly_region, poly_transects, lwd = 0.5, col = 4)

## Create Density

# Create a flat density grid
density <- make.density(region = study_region, x.space <http://x.space> = 1, constant = 1)

# Add hotspots to the density grid for spatial variability
density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(5, 5), sigma = 10, amplitude = 2)
density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(15, 25), sigma = 5, amplitude = 3)
density <- add.hotspot(object = density, centre = c(40, 15), sigma = 15, amplitude = -0.5)

# Plot the density grid
plot(density, study_region)

# Create population descriptions for the study area and subplots to test both
study_area_pop_desc <- make.population.description(region = study_region, density = density)

# Create a detectability function
detect_uf <- make.detectability(
  key.function = "uf",
  scale.param = 0.8,
  truncation = 2
)

plot(detect_uf, study_area_pop_desc)

# Create detection function analyses
ddf_analyses <- make.ds.analysis(dfmodel = ~1, key = c("hn", "hr"), criteria = "AIC", truncation = 2)

# Create a simulation for the subplots

sim <- make.simulation(
  reps = 99,
  design = poly_design,
  population.description = study_area_pop_desc,

  detectability = detect_uf,
  ds.analysis = ddf_analyses

)
# Run the survey and summarize the results

summary(sim, use.max.reps = TRUE, description.summary = FALSE) # here were no successful repetitions.

# Failing
survey <- run.survey(sim) # Error in sample.int <http://sample.int>(length(x), size, replace, prob) : incorrect number of probabilities

# Print the survey results

print(survey)

# Plot the survey results

> > # Define the outer boundary and holes for the polygons

> >

> >

> >

> >

> >

> >

> >

> >
> >

> > subplots_transects <- generate.transects(subplots_design)

> >
> >
